content: Iron(II) oxide, also referred to as ferrous oxide or ferrous iron, is one of the various oxides of iron. It appears as a black-colored powder and has the chemical formula FeO. This compound is composed of iron in its +2 oxidation state, chemically bonded to oxygen. In its natural mineral form, it is called wüstite, a term often used interchangeably with ferrous oxide. Iron(II) oxide is classified as a non-stoichiometric compound, meaning that the ratio of iron to oxygen atoms can vary due to the presence of crystallographic vacancies within its structure. This compound is highly unstable and prone to oxidation, readily converting into iron(III) oxide under certain conditions. It is important to distinguish iron(II) oxide from rust, as rust typically consists of hydrated iron(III) oxide, also known as ferric oxide. Iron(II) oxide is not the same as rust. Iron(II) oxide has practical applications, including its use as a pigment. It has been approved by the FDA for use in cosmetics and is also utilized in certain tattoo inks.
